newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - No big deal if Italy joins EMU late - Austria.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - No big deal if Italy joins EMU late - Austria.

text.p: The Austrian government said on Monday it was no big deal if Italy missed the start of Europe's currency union by one or two years, dampening the festive mood over Italy's belated return to the European exchange rate grid.

"It is not serious if Italy joins one or two years later," Finance Minister Viktor Klima told Austrian state radio. "But of course it is the goal of the Italian government as well as the European Union and Austria that Italy joins the euro-zone as soon as possible."

Italy rejoined the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM), intended as a precursor to Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), this weekend. The lira dropped out of the grid in 1992 following a sharp devaluation amid a wave of currency turmoil.

Klima, mirroring similar remarks by top German officials, said he welcomed the lira's return into the ERM, but insisted the move should not be seen as a sign Italy would automatically be among the founding members of EMU.
"All finance ministers agree that yesterday's decision was very important but that it was not prejudicial for a decision on who will be in the euro-zone," he said.

Like Austria, Italy is currently scrambling to put its finances in shape to qualify for the planned start of EMU in 1999. To join, countries must aim to meet strict goals on interest and exchange rates, inflation, deficits and public debt next year.

"No doubt it would be desirable for Austria if Italy, its second-biggest trading partner, were in the euro-zone from the start. But it is equally important, I would say even more important, that we have a stable euro," Klima added.

Austria joined the ERM last year. The country is seen as a strong candidate for early membership in EMU, even though its public debt level -- like that of most European Union members -- is projected to exceed the Maastricht Treaty's threshold.

The Austrian government earlier this year introduced a tough two-year austerity budget, aimed at pushing the public deficit to the targeted three percent of gross domestic product by next year from 4.3 percent this year.
Klima said Italy's return to the ERM should benefit Austria's strongly export-oriented industry by providing a better and more stable trading environment.
"We can all remember how the Austrian economy, how the job market suffered when Italy devalued massively in 1992," he said.

"For Austria's economy and thus for jobs it was extremely important that Italy returned to the ERM and that it joined with a stable exchange rate. Its a great chance for Austria's exporters," Klima added.

The lira was admitted at a central rate of 990 lira to the mark, corresponding to about 7.1 schillings for 1,000 lira. In 1992, the currency had crashed to as low as 5.50 schillings per 1,000 lira before it was forced out of the ERM.
